title: What percentage is that?
objectives: Express one quantity as a percentage of another
Choose the right whole for a comparison

screens.title: What percentage is that?
screens.prose: A test score, a win rate and a slice of a portfolio all compare a part with a whole. We will turn any such comparison into a percentage.
You scored 18 marks out of 25 on a test. Each of the 25 cells is one mark.
screens.question: What percentage did you score?

hints.text: The test is out of 25, not 100. How many hundredths of the square is one cell?
25 cells fill the square, so this one cell is 4 hundredths of it.
18 cells of 4 hundredths each is $18 \times 4 = 72$ hundredths.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Scale 25 marks up to 100, and the 18 with it.

byKey.raw: You gave the marks as the percentage. 18 out of 25 is more than 18 out of 100.
byKey.flipped: You divided 25 by 18. The part, 18, goes on top and the whole, 25, below.

explain.text: Each of the 25 cells is 4 hundredths, so 18 cells are $18 \times 4 = 72$ hundredths. You scaled the whole up to 100: $\tfrac{18}{25} = \tfrac{72}{100} = 72\%$. The dashed lines show the 100 hundredths.

screens.prose: A portfolio is split into 20 equal slices. The slider shades whole slices. Its number is the shaded part of the portfolio.
screens.question: Shade 7 of the 20 slices.

hints.text: One full row is 5 slices. You need one row and two more.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the shaded slices: you need 7.

explain.text: Seven slices of 20 read as 0.35 on the slider. That is $\tfrac{7}{20} = \tfrac{35}{100} = 35\%$. Each slice is 5%, because 20 slices share 100%.

screens.prose: You have been finding **one amount as a percentage of another**: the part over the whole, counted in hundredths. This rectangle has 50 cells, and 13 are shaded.
screens.question: What is 13 as a percentage of 50?

hints.text: 50 cells fill the whole. How many hundredths is each cell?
Two cells like this one would make 4 hundredths: each is 2.
Each cell is 2 hundredths, so 13 cells is 26 hundredths.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Scale 50 up to 100, and 13 with it.

byKey.raw: You gave the count as the percentage. 13 out of 50 is twice as big as 13 out of 100.
byKey.halved: You halved 13. To scale 50 up to 100 you double, so double 13 as well.

explain.text: Doubling 50 gives 100, so double 13 as well: $\tfrac{13}{50} = \tfrac{26}{100} = 26\%$. The part and the whole must be scaled by the same number.

screens.prose: A trader made 40 trades last month, one per cell. Nine of them lost money. 40 does not double or quadruple neatly to 100.
screens.question: What percentage of the trades lost money?

hints.text: When scaling to 100 is awkward, divide the part by the whole.
Nine shaded cells out of all 40.
$9 \div 40 = 0.225$, which is 22.5 hundredths.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the losing trades by all the trades.

byKey.raw: You gave the count as the percentage. 9 out of 40 is more than 9 out of 100.
byKey.flipped: You divided 40 by 9. The part goes on top: 9 divided by 40.

explain.text: Each of the 40 cells is 2.5 hundredths, so 9 cells is 22.5 hundredths. Dividing gets there directly: $9 \div 40 = 0.225 = 22.5\%$. Division works whatever the whole is.

screens.prose: A fund held £400 in cash at the start of the year. It now holds £500. Each cell is £100.
screens.question: What is the new cash as a percentage of the old cash?

widget.label: New cash as a percentage of old

hints.text: Which amount is the whole here? The question says of the old cash.
The old cash, four cells of £100, is the whole.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put the new cash over the old cash.

byKey.flipped: You divided the old by the new. The question measures the new cash against the old, so the old goes below.
byKey.rise: You gave the rise, £100 as a share of £400. The question asks for all of the new £500.

explain.text: The old £400 is the whole, so the new £500 is $\tfrac{500}{400} = 1.25 = 125\%$ of it. A part can be bigger than the whole it is measured against. Read the word after "of" to find the whole.

screens.prose: A savings rate rises from 4% to 5%. One headline says rates rose by 1%. Another says they rose by 25%.
screens.question: Which description is exact?

options.text: The rate rose by 1 percentage point, which is 25% of the old rate.
Both headlines describe the same change in the same way.
options.why: You treated 1% and 25% as one number in two units. One is a gap on the rate scale; the other compares it with 4%.

options.text: The rate rose by 25 percentage points.
options.why: You attached points to the relative change. A rise of 25 points would take the rate from 4% to 29%.

options.text: The rate rose by 1% of its old value.
options.why: 1% of the old 4% is only 0.04 points. The rate rose by a full point, a quarter of 4%.

hints.text: Measure the gap between 4% and 5% first.
The gap is 1 on a scale of percentages.
The gap, 1, as a share of the old 4 is $\tfrac{1}{4} = 25\%$.

feedback.correct: A gap of 1 point, which is a quarter of the old 4%.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the gap, then the gap as a share of the old rate.

explain.text: The gap between two percentages is measured in **percentage points**: $5\% - 4\% = 1$ point. As a share of the old rate, that point is $\tfrac{1}{4} = 25\%$. Both numbers are true, but they answer different questions.

canvas.caption: From 4% to 5%: 1 point, a quarter of 4%

screens.prose: A trader closed 15 winning trades and 10 losing trades this month. Solid cells are winners; hatched cells are losers.
screens.question: What percentage of the trades were winners?

options.why: You divided winners by losers. The whole is all 25 trades, not the 10 losers.
You divided losers by winners. Neither part is the whole: that is all 25 trades.
That is the share of losing trades, 10 of 25. The question asks about the winners.

hints.text: How many trades were there in total?
These 15 cells are the winners, out of all 25 cells.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The whole is every trade, winners and losers together.

byKey.ratio: You compared winners with losers. A percentage of the trades needs all 25 trades on the bottom.

explain.text: The whole is every trade: $15 + 10 = 25$. Winners over the whole is $\tfrac{15}{25} = 60\%$. Winners over losers answers a different question: 1.5 winners per loser.

screens.prose: Every time, you put the part over the whole and counted hundredths: $$\text{part as a percentage of whole} = \frac{\text{part}}{\text{whole}} \times 100\%$$ The whole is the amount after the word "of".
screens.question: Which calculation gives £6 as a percentage of £40?

options.why: You put the whole on top. That gives about 667%, far more than the whole.
You found 6% of £40. The question asks what percentage £6 is of £40.
You multiplied the part by the whole. A share of a whole needs a division.

hints.text: Which amount comes after the word of?
£40 is the whole, so it goes below: $\tfrac{6}{40} \times 100 = 15$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Part on top, whole below, then multiply by 100.

explain.text: £6 is the part and £40 the whole. $\tfrac{6}{40} = 0.15$, and multiplying by 100 counts hundredths: 15%.

screens.prose: Put the lines in order to find £18 as a percentage of £240.
screens.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.text: Write the part over the whole: $\tfrac{18}{240}$.
Divide top and bottom by 6 to simplify: $\tfrac{3}{40}$.

hints.text: Start by deciding which amount goes on top.
Fraction, simplify, divide, then multiply by 100.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each line must use the result of the one before.

explain.text: You set up $\tfrac{18}{240}$, simplified it to $\tfrac{3}{40}$, divided and counted hundredths. Simplifying first kept the division small. Check: 1% of £240 is £2.40, and $7.5 \times £2.40 = £18$.

screens.prose: Your portfolio holds four positions. A risk rule says no single position may exceed 30% of the portfolio.
screens.question: What percentage of the portfolio is Shares B?

widget.label: Shares B as a percentage of the portfolio

hints.text: The whole is the total value of the portfolio.
Shares B over the total.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the position by the total.

byKey.rest: You divided by the other three positions, £9,000. The whole is the total, £12,500.
byKey.largest: You compared B with Shares A. The whole is the total portfolio.

explain.text: $\tfrac{3{,}500}{12{,}500} = 0.28$, so Shares B is 28% of the portfolio. That is 2 percentage points inside the 30% limit. Shares A, at 32%, breaks it.

ideas: Put the part over the whole, then count hundredths.
The whole is the amount after the word "of"; a part can exceed it.
A gap between two percentages is in percentage points, not percent.

formula.name: One amount as a percentage of another
formula.note: The whole is every item, never just the other part.

summary.trap: 15 wins and 10 losses is a 60% win rate, not 150%. Divide by all the trades.

quiz.question: What is £45 as a percentage of £60?

byKey.raw: You gave £45 as the percentage. It is out of £60, not out of £100.
byKey.flipped: You divided £60 by £45. The part goes on top.

quiz.prose: A central bank cuts its rate from 3.5% to 2.5%.
quiz.question: By how many percentage points did the rate fall?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract the new rate from the old.

byKey.relative: You gave the fall as a percentage of the old rate. Points measure the plain gap: 3.5 minus 2.5.

explain.text: Percentage points measure the gap on the rate scale: $3.5\% - 2.5\% = 1$ point.

quiz.prose: The same rate falls from 3.5% to 2.5%.
quiz.question: As a percentage of the old rate, how big is the fall?

widget.label: Fall as a percentage of the old rate

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put the 1-point fall over the old 3.5.

byKey.points: You gave the fall in points. The question asks for it as a share of the old rate.
byKey.new-whole: You divided by the new rate, 2.5. Of the old rate means 3.5 goes below.

explain.text: The fall is 1 point and the old rate is 3.5. So the fall is $\tfrac{1}{3.5} \approx 0.286$, about 28.6% of the old rate.

quiz.prose: Over 40 trading days, a strategy was up on 26 days and down on 14.
quiz.question: What percentage of the days were up days?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the up days by all 40 days.

byKey.ratio: You divided up days by down days. The whole is all 40 days.
byKey.down: That is the share of down days. The question asks about up days.
